memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text:
"'You shall not covet your neighbor's house. You shall not covet your neighbor's
wife, or his male or female servant, his ox or donkey, or anything that belongs
to your neighbor.'" - Ex 20:17 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The tenth command is different from the other nine. Every other one can be
observed from outside. Nobody can see coveting.

This command goes into the heart, and in doing so it exposes what the whole law
was always driving at. God has never been satisfied with managed behaviour.

Notice how coveting works. It is not wanting something; wanting is human and
often good. It is wanting what is another's, and it feeds on comparison. The word
"neighbour" appears repeatedly here. Coveting requires someone to measure against.

That is why the modern world is such fertile ground for it. We now compare
ourselves not with the family next door but with thousands of curated lives, and
the ache never settles.

Paul says something striking about this specific command: "I would not have known
what coveting really was if the law had not said, 'You shall not covet'" (Rom
7:7). This is the command that showed him he could not keep the law at all.

That is the law's honest work. It shows us the disease. It cannot cure it.

The cure is contentment learned in Christ: "I have learned to be content whatever
the circumstances" (Phil 4:11). Learned. It comes slowly.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Whose life do you find yourself measuring your own against?
2. What would contentment look like for you this week?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Father, quiet the comparing in me. Teach me contentment and gratitude for what
You have given. Amen.
